asset.title: [Workflow demo] Citation Support vs. Citation Validity
asset.evidence_note: The provided notes directly address why an existing citation identifier can fail to support a claim, with the human-review example and the three-question framework in chunk 927abd040836438c9f6bf776c1ba13e6.
learning_objectives: Explain why a structurally valid citation identifier does not guarantee factual support for a claim [927abd040836438c9f6bf776c1ba13e6].
Apply the three-question citation-support check to a concrete example from the notes [927abd040836438c9f6bf776c1ba13e6].

sections.heading: A valid citation identifier is not the same as support
sections.text:
Citation support requires actually reading the cited text. An existing citation identifier only proves that a passage can be found in the recorded source set; it does not prove that the passage supports every sentence in the explanation [927abd040836438c9f6bf776c1ba13e6].

A concrete example from the notes: a passage stating that human review is required cannot support a generated claim that retrieval always eliminates mistakes. In this case the citation is structurally valid, but the factual conclusion is unsupported [927abd040836438c9f6bf776c1ba13e6].

To assess citation support, the notes separate three questions: (1) does the cited identifier belong to the passages supplied to this generation, (2) does that passage contain the information needed for the claim, and (3) does the explanation preserve any conditions or limitations in that information? A program can check only the first question mechanically; the second and third require a content judgment [927abd040836438c9f6bf776c1ba13e6].

questions.answer: An existing citation identifier only proves that a passage can be found in the recorded source set; it does not prove the passage supports every sentence of the explanation. For example, a passage stating that human review is required cannot support a generated claim that retrieval always eliminates mistakes: the citation is structurally valid but the factual conclusion is unsupported. The notes say to separate three questions: (1) does the cited identifier belong to the passages supplied to this generation; (2) does that passage contain the information needed for the claim; (3) does the explanation preserve any conditions or limitations in that information? Only the first can be checked mechanically; the second and third require a content judgment.
questions.explanation: A citation identifier is a structural record, not a factual guarantee. The notes give the human-review example: the cited passage requires human review, so it cannot support a claim that retrieval always eliminates mistakes. The three-question framework shows that identifier validity (question 1) is only the mechanical part; whether the passage contains the needed information (question 2) and whether conditions are preserved (question 3) require content judgment [927abd040836438c9f6bf776c1ba13e6].
questions.difficulty_reason: The learner must recall a concrete example from the notes, then apply a three-part conceptual distinction (identifier validity vs. content support vs. preserved limitations) to explain why the example fails. This is two-step reasoning within the given material.
